title: Bring your own power: Start with the development decision, not the technology
summary: BYOP can improve time to power, but it introduces new fuel, permitting, site, commercial, and operating constraints. A new framework helps data center developers determine when dedicated generation improves the overall development path.
body_markdown:
For many large data center and AI projects, securing power has become one of the most difficult parts of development. Grid-connection timelines are increasing in constrained markets, required upgrades can be extensive, and utilities are placing more technical and operating conditions on very large loads.


These pressures are driving growing interest in bring your own power (BYOP), dedicated onsite or adjacent prime power generation serving some or all of a data center's normal electrical load.


For some projects, BYOP can improve time to power, reduce dependence on constrained utility capacity, and provide greater control over energy availability. But it is not necessarily a shortcut around the grid. Dedicated generation introduces another set of requirements involving fuel, permitting, land, emissions, water, interconnection, equipment, capital, operations, and long-term asset risk.


The question, therefore, is not simply, "What generation technology should we use?"


A more fundamental question comes first: Does BYOP create a better development path for this project than the available alternatives?


That is the question addressed in our new white paper,[“A framework for evaluating bring your own power (BYOP) for data centers.”](https://www.vertiv.com/en-us/insights/articles/white-papers/when-grid-constraints-ask-is-byop-right-for-your-data-center/)


### Understand the utility option before trying to replace it


The first step is to determine what utility service can realistically provide. Available megawatts and an estimated energization date are only part of that assessment. Developers also need to understand what grid upgrades will be required, what studies and models must be provided, who pays for infrastructure improvements, what tariffs apply, and what operating conditions may be attached to service.


Those conditions can matter as much as available capacity. Phased energization, ramp-rate limits, curtailment provisions, demand response, telemetry requirements, fault ride-through requirements, or other operating commitments can affect the site's architecture, operating model, cost, and schedule.


The objective is to understand not only whether the utility can serve the load, but whether the terms of that service support the project.


### Compare the development paths, not just the power sources


If utility service does not meet the project's requirements, BYOP is still not automatically the next step.


Depending on the workload and business objectives, other options may include phasing development around available capacity, expanding an existing facility, moving to a less constrained market, using cloud or colocation capacity, or co-locating with an existing generation source.


These alternatives should be evaluated against common criteria such as capacity certainty, schedule, cost, operating control, permitting risk, utility requirements, complexity, public acceptance, and long-term flexibility.


The right answer may ultimately be BYOP. It may also be a combination of approaches that changes over the life of the project. What matters is whether dedicated generation reduces the project's overall risk rather than simply transferring the power challenge from the utility to the developer or a third-party provider.


### Define what BYOP must do before selecting how to generate power


If BYOP remains attractive after that comparison, the next decision is its intended role.


A system designed to bridge a temporary gap until utility power becomes available is fundamentally different from one intended to supplement constrained grid capacity over the long term. Both differ again from an islanded facility designed to operate without normal utility service.


Those use cases affect how long generation must operate, how it interacts with the grid, what redundancy and maintainability are required, how the facility transitions between operating modes, and what happens to the generation assets if utility conditions change.


They also influence which generation and fuel options make sense.


Selecting a technology first can produce a technically workable system that is poorly matched to the project's actual requirements.


### Test the constraints that can determine feasibility


Once the use case is understood, the evaluation needs to extend well beyond the generator itself.


Ownership, physical arrangement, and commercial structure are separate decisions. The data center may own and operate the generation, contract with an independent power producer, participate in an energy park, use an energy-as-a-service model, or employ another commercial structure. Each changes how capital, operational responsibility, performance risk, and control are allocated.


Site feasibility can be equally decisive. Dedicated generation can add power-plant-scale equipment, fuel infrastructure, electrical interconnection equipment, emissions controls, maintenance access, safety clearances, and other requirements to the project.


Fuel deserves particular attention. A natural gas pipeline near the site does not necessarily mean sufficient gas is available at the required volume, pressure, reliability, cost, or schedule. Pipeline laterals, metering, pressure regulation, compression, rights-of-way, permits, and utility upgrades can introduce their own project timelines.


A BYOP strategy intended to solve an electric-grid constraint can therefore encounter a different infrastructure constraint if fuel availability is not evaluated with the same rigor.


### Then evaluate technology and fuel


Technology selection should come after the project's use case, delivery model, and major site constraints are understood.


The generation system must be evaluated against requirements such as deployment time, capital and operating cost, fuel availability, redundancy, maintainability, emissions, permitting, scalability, power quality, and grid interaction.


For AI facilities, dynamic load behavior also matters. Rapid changes in power demand may require coordinated design and operation among generation, UPS systems, energy storage, and other parts of the electrical architecture. Different generation technologies also have different startup, cycling, part-load, and load-following characteristics.


There is no single technology answer for BYOP because there is no single BYOP application.


### The answer may still be no


The framework is presented in a logical sequence, but the process is inherently iterative.


A promising generation option may prove impractical because fuel cannot be secured. A commercially attractive solution may encounter permitting or land constraints. A workable onsite design may be less attractive once utility conditions improve. Findings later in the evaluation can and should cause developers to revisit earlier assumptions.


That is an important outcome of the process, not a failure of it.


BYOP should move forward when dedicated generation provides a more viable overall development path than the alternatives after its additional technical, commercial, permitting, fuel, site, and operating requirements are considered.


The goal is not to justify BYOP, it is to determine when BYOP is justified.
